title: Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome
statement: You are given a string `s`. A single move adds one character of your choice at any position of the string (the front, the end, or between two characters). Return the fewest moves needed to turn `s` into a palindrome, a string equal to its own reverse.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Look only at the two ends of a piece of the string. If they match, they already mirror each other, and the work left is whatever the inside needs. If they differ, one of them must be mirrored by a newly inserted character: either insert a copy of the left end on the right side (then solve the piece without the left end) or a copy of the right end on the left (then solve it without the right end). Each choice costs one move, so take the cheaper. These answers for shorter pieces build the answer for longer ones, which is interval dynamic programming. Equivalently, the answer is `n` minus the longest palindromic subsequence, which is what the brute-force check computes.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i][j]` be the fewest insertions that make `s[i..j]` a palindrome. Single characters and empty pieces need 0, so the table starts at 0.
2. Fill rows from `i = n - 2` down to 0, and in each row `j` from `i + 1` up, so the shorter pieces `dp[i + 1][...]` and `dp[i][j - 1]` are ready.
3. If `s[i] === s[j]`, copy `dp[i + 1][j - 1]`.
4. Otherwise take `1 + Math.min(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])`.
5. Return `dp[0][n - 1]`, the answer for the whole string.

## Example 1, step by step

For `s = "zzazz"`, the inner piece `"a"` (`dp[2][2]`) needs 0. `"zaz"` has matching ends `z` and `z`, so `dp[1][3] = dp[2][2] = 0`. The full string has matching ends as well, so `dp[0][4] = dp[1][3] = 0`: no insertions are needed.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every pair `i < j` is filled once in constant time.
- Space: O(n²) for the table (one row of the previous `i` would be enough).

## Pitfalls

- Fill order matters: `i` must go downward so that `dp[i + 1][...]` is already computed.
- For two equal neighbours (`j = i + 1`), `dp[i + 1][j - 1]` refers to an empty piece; it is 0 because the table starts filled with 0.
- Greedily inserting at the first mismatch is wrong; both options must be compared.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `dp[i][j]` | fewest insertions that make `s[i..j]` a palindrome |
| `i`, `j` | left and right ends of the current piece |

narration.3: Build an n by n table of zeros; a piece of length 0 or 1 needs no insertions.
narration.4: Start from the second-to-last position so the row below is always ready.
narration.5: Extend the piece to every right end j after i.
narration.6: Do the two ends of s[i..j] match?
narration.7: Yes: they mirror each other, so only the inside s[i+1..j-1] needs work.
narration.9: No: insert a mirror for one end and solve the rest, whichever is cheaper.
narration.13: The whole string s[0..n-1] holds the final answer.
